---
title: "Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations of Carbon Nano-Systems"
abstract: |
  "The strongly-correlated behavior of electrons in low dimensional systems, such as TMDs or graphene and its derivatives, require non-perturbative methods ideally suited for lattice quantum monte carlo (QMC) methods.  I provide an introduction to QMC and discuss how it is used to simulate these low-dimensional systems to ascertain their electronic properties.  At the same time, I show how the relatively small dimensions of these systems offer ideal platforms for developing novel algorithms, such as "contour deformations" and "radial updates".  The former alleviates the sign problem, allowing for simulations at non-zero chemical potential, while the latter removes ergodicity issues and thus mitigates critical slowing down.  Finally I discuss how QMC methods can be used to investigate the topological properties of these systems, which could have impact in their usage as novel quantum devices. "
author:

# Why use QMC?
  
## ***Curse of Dimensionality***

+ Consider a simple 1-d integral using Simpson's $k=4$ rule

  $$
  \int_a^b dx f(x) = \frac{h}{3}\left(f_0+4f_1+2f_2+\cdots+4f_{N-1}+f_N\right)\quad;\quad h=\frac{b-a}{N},\ f_i=f(x_i)
  $$

  convergence of this integral $\sim\mathcal{O}(N^{-k})$
  
+ In $d$ dimensions, convergence scales as $\sim\mathcal{O}(N^{-k/d})$

+ Example of deterministic ("grid-based") 

:::{.callout-note .fragment}
## How do we refine out calculation?
:::

## Refining our deterministic calculation

:::{.fragment}

+ Increase the number of "integration points" to increase accuracy

+ Let's double our accuracy$\implies N\to N'=2^d N$

| d      | 10   | 20      | 30         |
|:------:|:----:|:-------:|:----------:|
| $N'/N$ | 1024 | 1048576 | 1073741824 |

:::

:::{.callout-warning .fragment}
## Example: molecular dynamics calculations of molecules in 1 cm$^3$ volume

$$ \mathrm{\#\  of\  particles\ } N\approx 10^{23}\implies \mathrm{phase\  space\  dimension\ } \Pi_i dx_i dp_i\sim 6N = d $$

:::

:::{.r-stack .fragment}

Good luck!

:::

## Lifting the curse

![](assets/enterMC.png){fig-align='center'}

:::{.r-stack}
Enter Monte Carlo
:::

+ Instead of calculating an observable ***deterministically***, we estimate an observable ***stochastically***


:::{.callout-important .fragment}
## The price we pay is that our ***estimate*** has an associated ***uncertainty***
:::

## Simplest example of MC estimate

:::{.r-stack}
![](assets/estimatePI1.png){fig-align='center'}

![](assets/estimatePI2.png){fig-align='center' .fragment}
:::

+ Estimate of $\pi$

 $$ \pi = 4\frac{\mathrm{area\ of\ circle}}{\mathrm{area\ of\ square}}\approx 4 \frac{\mathrm{\#\ red\ points}}{\mathrm{\#\ of\ red\ \&\ blue\ points}} $$


## Advantages of (Q)MC

+ Ideal for high-dimensional spaces

+ Valid for both weakly and strongly interacting systems
  - independent of complexity of problem!

+ Error of estimate scales with number of samples $N_{\mathrm{cfg}}$ as $\mathcal{O}(N_{\mathrm{cfg}}^{-1/2})$
  - controllable and systematic
  - independent of dimension $d$
  
:::{.callout-warning .fragment}
## But. . .

:::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

+ Requires big computers
+ Noisy estimates
+ Can obtain biased results
  - non-ergodic
+ Infamous numerical ***sign-problem***

:::

## Hamiltonian

:::{style='font-size:80%'}
+ General Hamiltonian is of the form

$$
  H
	= 
	\sum_{yx} \left(p^\dagger_y K_{yx} p_x + h^\dagger_y K_{yx} h_x \right)
	+ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{yx} \rho_y V_{yx} \rho_x
	- \mu \sum_x \rho_x
$$

+ $\rho_x\equiv p_x^\dagger p_x^{}-h_x^\dagger h_x^{}$ (particle and hole creation/annihilation operators)
   
:::
:::{.columns .fragment}

:::{.column width="60%"}

:::{style='font-size:80%'}

:::{.callout-note}
## The Hubbard model

For most of the work presented here we use tight-binding dynamics and Hubbard onsite interaction:

\begin{align}
	K_{xy} &= \kappa \delta_{\langle xy \rangle}
	&
	V_{xy} &= U \delta_{xy}.
	\label{eq:hubbard}
\end{align}

:::

:::

:::

:::{.column width="40%"}

![](assets/intro_lattice.png){fig-align="center"}

:::

:::

##  Attempting a direct diagonalization of $H$

![](assets/intro_lattice.png){fig-align='center'}

$N_x=72$ sites

:::{.callout-warning}
## Full diagonalization of this problem

Dimensionality of the problem scales as $4^{N_x}$

Example: $4^{72}=22300745198530623141535718272648361505980416$

:::

## First steps towards Quantum Monte Carlo

Instead of diagonalizing $H$, we concentrate on obtaining thermal expectation values of any operator $O$

$$
  \langle O \rangle = \frac{1}{Z}\mathrm{Tr}\  Oe^{-\beta H}
$$

where $\beta=1/T$ is in inverse temperature and 

$$
Z=\mathrm{Tr}\ e^{-\beta H}
$$

is the ***partition function***.

The trace is performed over the entire ***Fock space***

:::{.callout-warning .fragment}
## Have we gained anything

Not really. . .

:::

## Introduce Auxiliary Field $\phi$


![](assets/PI_formalism.png){fig-align='center'}

:::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.callout-note .fragment}
## Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation

$$e^{-\frac{\delta U}{2}\rho_{x,t}^2}\propto\int d\phi_{x,t}e^{-\frac{\phi_{x,t}^2}{2\delta U}+i\phi_{x,t}\rho_{x,t}}$$

"Linearized" the density term

:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.callout-note .fragment}
## Integration measure $\mathcal{D}[\phi]$

$$\int \mathcal{D}[\phi]=\int\Pi_{x,t}d\phi_{x,t}$$

High-dimensional integral!!  Enter Monte Carlo. . .

:::

:::

:::

## Feynman's Path Integral

$$ \langle O\rangle = \int\mathcal{D}[\phi]O[\phi]\frac{e^{-S[\phi]}}{Z}= \int\mathcal{D}[\phi]O[\phi]\mathbb{P}[\phi]$$

![](assets/PI.png){fig-align='center'}

:::{.callout-important .fragment}
## Importance Sampling
Not all paths are equally important!  Want to ***sample*** most relevant paths dictated by $\mathbb{P}[\phi]$.
:::

### Sign-problem free

+ bipartite lattice

$\implies$ NO SIGN PROBLEM!

## Anatomy of a QMC simulation

:::{style='font-size:80%'}

:::{.fragment}
+ Generate ***ensemble*** of field configurations $\phi_i\in\{\phi\}$ stochastically where 
  $$ \mathbb{P}[\phi_i]\sim e^{-S[\phi_i]}/Z $$
:::

:::{.fragment}
+ Estimate $\langle O\rangle$ 
  $$ \langle O\rangle = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{cfg}}}\sum_{\phi_i\in\{\phi\}}O[\phi_i] + \mathcal{O}(N_{\mathrm{cfg}}^{-1/2}) $$
  
  - Perform error analysis
    - Determine autocorrelation
    - bootstrap errors
:::

:::{.fragment}
+ Perform limit extrapolations
  - continuum $\delta\to 0$
  - thermodynamic $N_x\to\infty$
  - zero-temperature $\beta\to\infty$
  - $m_\pi\to m_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}$ (LQCD)
:::  

:::

# What observables $O$ are we interested in?

## Anatomy of a correlator

Single-body correlation functions $\langle p_x^{}(\tau)p_y^\dagger(0)\rangle = \langle M_{xy;\tau}^{-1}\rangle\equiv C(\tau)$

![](assets/correlator.png){fig-align="center" height=4in}

:::{.callout-note}
## Spectral Decomposition Theorem
\begin{align}
C(\tau)&=A_p e^{-(E_p-E_\Omega)\tau}+A_{ex} e^{-(E_{ex}-E_\Omega)\tau}+\ldots+A_he^{(E_h-E_\Omega)(\tau-\beta)}\\
&\to A_pe^{-(E_p-E_\Omega)\tau}\quad\quad(0\ll\tau\ll\beta)
\end{align}
:::

### Excitons {.center}

  - particle-hole excitations 
    * "bright" excitons
	* "dark" excitons
  - analogous to pions in lattice QCD
  - $I_z=0,S_z=1$ correlation function: $\frac{1}{2}\langle\left(p_i^\dagger h_j^\dagger + h_i^\dagger p_j^\dagger \right)\left( h_k^{} p_l^{} + p_k^{} h_l^{} \right)\rangle
=\langle M^{-1\ast}_{ki;\tau}M^{-1}_{lj;\tau}+M^{-1\ast}_{li;\tau}M^{-1}_{kj;\tau}\rangle$
  - Are "dark" excitons bound? P. Sinilkov, **T.L.**, et al., [PoS LATTICE2024 (2025) 075](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04015)

# The "Sign Problem"

## Complex Action $S[\phi]$

:::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

+ Probability only makes sense when
  $$
  \mathbb{P}[\phi]=\frac{e^{-S[\phi]}}{Z}\in \mathbb{R}_+ \implies S[\phi]\in \mathbb{R}
  $$

+ $\exists$ systems when $S[\phi]\in \mathbb{C}$
  + non-bipartite lattice
	- cannot divide system into sublattices
   + non-zero chemical potential $\mu\ne0$
	 - doping (away from half-filling)
	 - QCD at finite baryon density
	 
	 
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.callout-important .fragment}

Most interesting problems have a sign problem!

+ Phase transitions at finite density (e.g. hardonic matter to quark/gluon plasma)
+ Doped Mott-Insulators (e.g. high-$T_c$ superconductivity)
+ Frustrated systems (quantum spin-systems on non-bipartite lattices)
+ Real-time evolution (e.g. non-equilibrium processes)
:::

:::{.callout-note .fragment}
## Reweighting
\begin{align}
	\langle O\rangle &= \frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}\int \mathcal{D}[\phi]\ O[\phi]\; e^{-S_{\mathcal{R}}[\phi]-iS_{\mathcal{I}}[\phi]}\\
	&=\frac{\int \mathcal{D}[\phi]\; O[\phi]e^{-iS_{\mathcal{I}}[\phi]}e^{-S_{\mathcal{R}}[\phi]}}{\int D\phi\; e^{-S_{\mathcal{R}}[\phi]}}\frac{\int D\phi\; e^{-S_{\mathcal{R}}[\phi]}}{\int D\phi\; e^{-S_{\mathcal{R}}[\phi]-iS_{\mathcal{I}}[\phi]}}\\
	&=\frac{\langle Oe^{-iS_{\mathcal{I}}}\rangle_{\mathcal{R}}}{\langle e^{-iS_{\mathcal{I}}}\rangle_{\mathcal{R}}}
	\quad;\quad\mbox{"average phase"}\  =\ \langle e^{-iS_{\mathcal{I}}}\rangle
\end{align}
:::

:::

:::

## Alleviating the Sign Problem w/ Contour deformations

Push domain of $\phi\in\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{C}^N$ 

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Lefschtz thimbles
:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
+ $\exists$ certain manifolds $\mathcal{T}\subset\mathbb{C}^N$ where $S_{\mathcal{I}}[\phi\in\mathcal{T}]={\rm constant}$
:::

\begin{align}
\int_{\phi\in\mathbb{R}^N}&\mathcal{D}[\phi]e^{-S[\phi]}\\
\to&
\sum_{\mathcal{T}}e^{-iS_{\mathcal{I}}^{\mathcal{T}}}\int_{\varphi\in\mathcal{T}\subset\mathbb{C}^N}\mathcal{D}[\varphi]e^{-S_{\mathcal{R}}[\varphi]}
\end{align}

:::

::: {.column width="10%"}

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![](assets/LefschetzThimble.png){fig-align="right"}

:::

:::

+ M. Cristoforetti et al., [Phys.Rev. D88 (2013) 051501](https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.7204)
+ Kanazawa & Tanizaki [JHEP 1503 (2015) 044](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.2802)


### "Learning" manifolds

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}
+ Location of thimbles not know *a priori*
  - Can approach thimbles via holomorphic flow
  - However, determining exact locations of all relevant thimbles just as hard as original sign problem
  - Numerically intensive
+ Train a NN to "learn" location of Lefschetz thimbles
:::

![](assets/ML_LT.png){fig-align="center"}

:::{style='font-size:60%'}
+ J.-L. Wynen, **T.L.**, et al., [Phys.Rev.B 103 (2021) 125153](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11221)
+ M. Rodekamp, **T.L.**, et al., [Phys.Rev.B 106 (2022) 125139](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00390)
:::

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

![](assets/ML_correlators2.png){fig-align="center"}

:::

:::

## Recapitulation

+ The ***Curse of Dimensionality*** and strongly-interacting systems drive the need for QMC

+ Low-D systems are ideal for QMC
  - Quasi multi-particle excitations above the bulk ground state
  - Localization of topological states w/ interactions
  
+ Excellent algorithmic development already done within the LQCD community
  - HMC
  - pseudo-fermions
  - preconditioners
  
+ Development of algorithms to ***alleviate*** the sign problem
  - adaption of machine learning techniques
  - normalizing flows
